Consonantal i

SearchHow we decideRulings

Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

consist of verb

also be made up of, be composed of, comprise, consist

classical

Cic. N.D. 1.98: homō ex animō cōnstat et corpore (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 245, 296: cōnstāre ex

cōnstō, cōnstāre, cōnstitī, cōnstātūrus

verb, first conjugation, intransitive, with ex and the ablative

consist of, be made up of

In Cicero always with ex (Lewis & Short). The verb has other common senses: to stand firm, to be consistent (sibi cōnstāre), to cost (with the genitive or ablative of price), and, impersonally, cōnstat, “it is agreed, everyone knows”.

Examples

  • homō ex animō cōnstat et corpore

    a human being consists of soul and bodyCic. N.D. 1.98 (Lewis & Short)

  • simplex ē dulcī cōnstat olīvō

    the plain (sauce) consists of sweet olive oilHor. S. 2.4.64 (Lewis & Short)

  • Ex quibus rēbus cōnstat haec placenta?

    What is this cake made of?composed

See also consist in, include, involve, of.

SourcesLewis & Short: consto

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 245, 296, checked against the searchable text of the book (11 November 2026).

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.

The example sentences marked “composed” are ours.
